approaches.name: Medial approach to the calcaneus
approaches.corridor: Interval between the posterior tibial neurovascular bundle and flexor hallucis longus to the sustentaculum tali and medial calcaneal wall

procedure_applications.condition: A displaced sustentaculum-tali fragment or medial-wall target requires direct reduction
A medial open wound requires debridement and direct medial access

positioning.text: Position supine with the hip externally rotated or use a bump so the medial hindfoot faces upward and remains accessible to imaging.

setup.text: Prep the leg and foot freely and confirm that lateral and axial heel fluoroscopic views can be obtained before incision.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the medial malleolus, navicular, sustentaculum tali, posterior tibial tendon, and anticipated course of the tarsal-tunnel neurovascular bundle.

incision.text: Place an approximately 5-cm incision parallel to the neurovascular bundle, centered inferior to the medial malleolus and directed toward the proximal navicular.

superficial_interval.text: Open flexor retinaculum and identify posterior tibial tendon, flexor digitorum longus, posterior tibial vessels and nerve, and flexor hallucis longus before developing a deep window.

deep_interval.text: Develop the interval between the posterior tibial neurovascular bundle and flexor hallucis longus, retracting FHL plantarly to expose sustentaculum and medial calcaneal wall.

layers.text: Skin and subcutaneous tissue, flexor retinaculum, identified tarsal-tunnel tendons and neurovascular bundle, interval beside FHL, then medial calcaneal periosteum and sustentaculum.

structures_encountered.text: Posterior tibial tendon, flexor digitorum longus, posterior tibial artery/veins and tibial nerve, flexor hallucis longus, sustentaculum tali, and deltoid-ligament fibers define the field.

structures_at_risk.text: The posterior tibial neurovascular bundle, medial calcaneal nerve branches, nerve to abductor digiti minimi, and flexor hallucis longus are at risk during exposure and fixation.

danger_zones.text: Do not create a blind window across the neurovascular bundle; identify every tarsal-tunnel structure and protect the bundle before working on either side of FHL.

retraction_hazards.text: Use gentle, intermittent retraction of the tibial neurovascular bundle and FHL and avoid fixed pressure within the confined tarsal tunnel.

exposure.text: Directly exposes the sustentaculum tali and medial/inferomedial calcaneal wall but does not provide the broad posterior-facet visualization of lateral approaches.

limitations.text: This is a targeted medial exposure for uncommon sustentacular or medial-wall pathology; most calcaneal fracture patterns are better addressed laterally or posteriorly.

extensions.text: Additional carefully separated windows may be developed around FHL and the protected bundle when fracture geometry requires more medial-wall access.

indications.text: Indicated for displaced sustentaculum-tali fractures, selected medial-wall reduction, and debridement of medial open calcaneal fractures.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid using this limited corridor as the sole exposure when posterior-facet, lateral-wall, or calcaneal-body reduction cannot be verified medially.

implant_implications.text: Plan screw and plate trajectories around the tibial neurovascular bundle and FHL and confirm that fixation does not penetrate the subtalar joint.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use image intensification to localize the sustentaculum and verify reduction, screw trajectory, and avoidance of subtalar penetration.

closure.text: Release retractors and confirm neurovascular integrity, repair flexor retinaculum when appropriate, and close subcutaneous tissue and skin without tension.

complications.text: Complications include tibial or medial-calcaneal neuropathy, posterior tibial vascular injury, FHL injury or tethering, medial instability, wound problems, and intra-articular fixation.

bailouts.text: If neurovascular mobilization is unsafe or reduction cannot be assessed, stop blind medial work and add the fracture-appropriate lateral or posterior exposure.

questions.question: What interval reaches the sustentaculum through the medial approach?
questions.answer: Between the posterior tibial neurovascular bundle and flexor hallucis longus.

questions.question: Which ligamentous fibers should be preserved to avoid medial instability and protect talar blood supply?
questions.answer: The tibiocalcaneal portion of the deltoid ligament.

approaches.name: Sinus tarsi approach to the calcaneus
approaches.corridor: Limited lateral interval from fibular tip toward fourth-metatarsal base, superior to the peroneal tendons, entering the sinus tarsi and posterior subtalar facet

sources.title: Sinus Tarsi Approach for Calcaneal Fractures: The New Gold Standard?

procedure_applications.condition: A displaced intra-articular fracture is reducible through a limited lateral articular window with adjunctive body reduction

positioning.text: Position lateral or floppy lateral with the operative hindfoot uppermost and the foot accessible for traction, reduction, and fluoroscopy.

setup.text: Respect soft-tissue timing and generally wait for recovery of lateral skin wrinkling; prepare an adjunctive reduction method for the calcaneal body and primary fracture line.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the fibular tip, base of the fourth metatarsal, peroneal-tendon course, sural-nerve region, and subtalar joint line.

incision.text: Make a limited incision from the fibular tip toward the fourth-metatarsal base, adjusting length and orientation to the fracture while avoiding posterior extension toward the sural nerve.

superficial_interval.text: Open deep fascia, protect the sural nerve and peroneal tendons inferiorly, and reflect only the necessary portion of extensor digitorum brevis.

deep_interval.text: Enter the sinus tarsi and subtalar capsule to visualize the posterior facet; preserve the deep superior peroneal retinaculum if proximal extension is required.

layers.text: Skin and subcutaneous tissue, deep fascia, protected sural nerve/peroneal tendons, limited extensor-digitorum-brevis reflection, sinus-tarsi capsule, then posterior subtalar facet.

structures_encountered.text: Sural nerve, peroneal tendons and retinacula, extensor digitorum brevis, lateral calcaneal artery territory, sinus-tarsi contents, and posterior facet define the approach.

structures_at_risk.text: The sural nerve and peroneal tendons are at risk inferiorly, while proximal violation of the deep superior peroneal retinaculum can endanger the lateral calcaneal artery and skin perfusion.

danger_zones.text: Avoid extending posterior to the lateral malleolus without identifying the sural-nerve course, and avoid deep proximal retinacular dissection that compromises lateral calcaneal blood supply.

retraction_hazards.text: Retract peroneal tendons and sural nerve gently and intermittently; do not lever forcefully through the small window to compensate for inadequate body-fragment reduction.

exposure.text: Provides direct visualization of the posterior subtalar facet and anterior calcaneus through a limited incision, with less visualization of the posterior body and primary fracture line.

limitations.text: The calcaneal body and primary fracture line are not directly visualized; an external fixator, Schanz pin, percutaneous manipulation, or other adjunct is needed for body reduction.

extensions.text: Lengthen distally along the lateral utility line for selected anterior-process or calcaneocuboid involvement while preserving lateral soft-tissue perfusion.

indications.text: Used for selected displaced intra-articular calcaneal fractures when posterior-facet reduction and fixation can be achieved through a limited lateral window.

relative_contraindications.text: Choose another exposure when fracture morphology demands broad direct body or posterior visualization, when the facet cannot be reduced through the window, or when lateral skin remains compromised.

implant_implications.text: Low-profile fixation can pass through the incision, but plate position, peroneal-tendon clearance, screw length, and subtalar penetration require imaging because body visualization is limited.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use lateral, axial heel, and Broden-type views to verify body reduction, posterior-facet congruity, width, alignment, and extra-articular screw placement.

closure.text: Replace reflected extensor tissue, close deep fascia with absorbable suture, and perform tension-free subcuticular or interrupted skin closure.

complications.text: Complications include sural neuropathy, wound necrosis or infection, peroneal injury or subluxation, residual body malreduction, subtalar incongruity, and symptomatic fixation.

bailouts.text: If body or articular reduction cannot be verified, add percutaneous reduction tools, arthroscopy, or the preplanned alternative exposure rather than accepting unseen malreduction.

questions.question: What portion of a calcaneal fracture is poorly visualized through the sinus-tarsi approach?
questions.answer: The posterior calcaneal body and the primary fracture line.

questions.question: What is the incision trajectory?
questions.answer: From the fibular tip toward the base of the fourth metatarsal.

questions.question: Which structures are protected inferior to the incision?
questions.answer: The sural nerve and peroneal tendons.
